In Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests.

Look closely at the lodgings that make up Dawn Ranch and you’ll notice they’re actually a patchwork of historic structures in different shapes and sizes. Each building at the luxe 15-acre Russian River resort, which is nestled amongst the towering redwoods in the petite town of Guerneville, California, is linked to a different era of the property’s past.

Built in 1905, it was originally Murphy’s Ranch, a getaway for well-to-do families that operated for seven decades. Later it served for more than 20 years as the pioneering gay resort Fife’s. Today, it’s a refined wine country escape that exists at the crossroads of nature and high-end luxury. The hotel is situated in a floodway, which limits construction for safety purposes, so since 1993 the site’s various owners haven’t been able to build anew; renovating ad infinitum has proven to be just dandy though.

In fact, this limitation turns out to be central to Dawn Ranch’s retro, summer camp-adjacent charm, which feels like a happy throwback even with its modernized facilities and amenities. Spectacularly refurbished in 2023, the current upscale iteration features 81 California-cool rooms, a tremendous spa, a fine-dining restaurant that may very well become impossible to book once word gets out, and a thoughtful, dynamic wine program that highlights some of the world’s most unique bottles.

Rachel Tepper Paley

Rachel Tepper Paley

The property and rooms

When it comes to bunking, you have choices that span a hodgepodge of rustic-chic cabins, chalets, cottages, bungalows, and glamping tents. On the main campus, cabins are cozy and compact, while the cottages and chalets offer more space. Most include private outdoor decks, equally ideal for taking in a morning cuppa or an evening tipple. The bungalows are the roomiest accommodation, outfitted for families and large groups with two bedrooms, two baths, a full kitchen, and gas fireplaces. Across the street, the resort’s Grove campus offers more options, which range from snug single-room affairs to spacious two bedrooms.

They’re all scattered amongst the tree-filled property’s sycamores and redwoods, so traipsing to your room feels like a walk in the forest. Inside, the aesthetic is a study in NorCal quiet luxury, with plenty of smooth blonde wood, layered textiles, and eclectic furniture pieces, plus Parachute linens and Le Labo bath goodies.

More adventurous guests will appreciate the smartly furnished glamping tents, situated in Dawn Ranch’s 120-year-old apple tree orchard. The walls may be canvas, but the beds feature the same Bear hybrid mattresses as those in Dawn Ranch’s more conventional rooms. You will, however, have to share a bathhouse—albeit an extremely nice one—with your fellower glampers.

No matter where you sleep, make sure you lay eyes on the resort’s namesake, a 70-year-old pair of rare dawn redwoods located near the pool on the main campus.

The restaurants and dining experience

The Lodge at Dawn Ranch, which houses the hotel’s main dining, bar, and lounge areas, manages a laid-back vibe that nonetheless feels rarefied and celebratory, with plush mauve-colored banquettes and dim romantic lighting.

But food is the real draw: Co-executive chefs (and husband-and-wife team) Ignacio “Nacho” Zuzulich and Juliana Thorpe center a nine-course, $155 tasting menu informed both by their respective Argentinian and Brazilian backgrounds and their experience cooking in lauded kitchens from Mugaritz in Spain to Napa Valley’s Meadowood resort. A truncated version of the tasting menu is served at the bar for $90.

Seasonal Golden State ingredients take top billing. On a recent visit, corn was a standout, taking the form of a delicate tostada set atop a fire-roasted corn custard. Festooned with the marigold-like flowering herb huacatay, it conveyed an impossibly large, flawless lobe of Santa Barbara uni.

In the morning, don’t skip breakfast at the Lodge, which is best taken on the sprawling outside deck. Soft scrambled eggs with avocado and furikake on homemade brioche are straightforward but deeply effective, while the cinnamon rolls glossed in cream cheese frosting are the perfect excuse to eat dessert before noon.

Rachel Tepper Paley

Rachel Tepper Paley

The inside scoop

When drinking, whether in the dining room or bar, vino is the move. This is wine country, after all. The handwritten “Sommelier’s Notebook” dispenses with formality, breaking wines into playful categories like “The Wild Ones,” “Extrovert Whites,” and “Quiet Elegance.” You’ll have plenty of fun ordering by the bottle or glass; if you’re after just a taste, some offerings are available in one-ounce pours.

But for the deep-pocketed, the $400 Decades Wine Pairing is a voyage through time and space, guiding you through wines bottled across generations. The offerings frequently shift, but this past summer, the oldest pour was an intensely molasses-forward D'Oliveiras Verdelho Madeira, first put under cork in 1891.

With its decadent syrup-like texture and vibrant acidity, the Madeira made for a complex complement to the tasting menu’s show-stopping dessert course, which presented local peaches in three manners: a quenelle of peach sorbet; a crystal cupful of peach nectar; and a tart of roasted peach jam and white chocolate ganache, topped with intricately woven, paper-thin peach slivers and served alongside a peach sabayon.

Best of all, returning to my cottage after dinner required only a brief, tipsy walk through the redwoods, the stars lighting my way.

Rachel Tepper Paley

This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Pre Shift: What did you want to explore with Muhājir that you hadn’t been able to do yet with your previous restaurants?

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from.

At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me.

Why did you decide to build the restaurant around live fire?

I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire.

Is there a dish that feels especially representative of Muhājir?

We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire.

When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration.

You have a bar called Bobo behind the restaurant. How do the two spaces complement each other?

Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun.

If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?”

What has it been like to run Muhājir so far?

I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition.

I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.”

This interview has been edited and condensed.

items.text:
Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.


Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.


I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.


Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.


In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Day 1: Immersion in the Art Walk


This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.


The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.


Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.


After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.


After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.


Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.


In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.


Day 2: The Grandeur of the Historic Center


The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.


Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).


From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.


For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.


After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.


To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.


Day 3: Culinary Discovery


Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.


If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.


For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.


As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.


For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.


Day 4: UNESCO World Heritage Wonders


Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.


One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.


Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.


Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).


Day 5: Off-the-Beaten-Path Treasures


On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.


The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.


The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).


To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.


***


While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

items.title: Don’t Visit Ko Lipe
items.author: Matthew Kepnes
items.summary: After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path
items.text:
After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.


There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.


It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.


If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.


Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.


Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.


And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.


But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.


And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.


So, I sucked it up and went.


And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Unsustainably so.


Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.


The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.


So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.


I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.


And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”


But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”


But this is not the way.


And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.


A visit there will only make things worse.


It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.


And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.


Go somewhere else that is better managed.


Because your choices do have an impact.


Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.


Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.


I doubt it but one can hope.


But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

blocks.x: After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.
It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.
Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.
And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.
But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.
So, I sucked it up and went.
And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.
Unsustainably so.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.
So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.
And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”
But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”
But this is not the way.
And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.
A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.
And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.
Go somewhere else that is better managed.
Because your choices do have an impact.
Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.
Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.
I doubt it but one can hope.
But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

items.text:
10月22日，A股三大指数集体下挫、全天弱势调整，创业板指低开低走，午后跌幅扩大，最终跌4.37%失守2600点，较今年6月的历史高点跌幅超40%。沪指、创业板指盘中均刷新2025年8月以来低点临近收盘，以沪深300ETF为代表的多只宽基ETF成交额激增。从全天成交额来看，4只宽基ETF成交额超过百亿元。

板块个股方面，AI硬件全线调整，光通信、电路板、覆铜板、光模块等概念股跌幅居前，新易盛、中际旭创、天孚通信等大幅下跌。创新药、CRO等亦大跌。机器人逆势拉升。银行整体稳健，央企银行走强，工商银行、建设银行双双刷新高位。

港股全天大幅下跌，恒指、恒科指午后扩大跌幅，恒指跌超3%，恒科指跌超5%，失守3800点，权重科网股、芯片半导体、AI大模型、生物医药、新能源汽车等几乎所有板块都下跌，光通信板块跌幅居前，长飞光纤光缆跌逾10%，中际旭创跌7%，剑桥科技、华虹宏力、海光芯正至少跌超9。债市方面，国债期货震荡下跌。商品方面，国内商品期货多数下跌。

A股：截至收盘，沪指跌1.48%，深成指跌2.96%，创业板指跌4.37%。

盘面上，个股跌多涨少，沪深京三市近5000股飘绿，今日成交1.54万亿。沪深两市成交额1.53万亿，较上一个交易日放量近1000亿。板块方面，覆铜板、光通信、CRO、传媒、海运板块领跌，房地产、农业、军工、煤炭板块走软。权重央企股逆市活跃，工行、建行创新高。

港股：截至收盘，恒指收跌3.03%，科指收跌5.03%。

盘面上，科网股、半导体产业、人工智能主题、创新药板块深度调整，联想集团跌超10%，华虹宏力跌9.5%，药明生物跌8.4%，阿里巴巴跌超6%。宁德时代跌约7%，布鲁可跌约21%，富力地产跌约12%，联想集团跌约11%，凯莱英跌约11%，世茂集团跌10%。

债市：国债期货震荡下跌，截至收盘，30年期主力合约跌0.19%，10年期主力合约持平，5年期主力合约持平，2年期主力合约持平。

商品：国内商品期货多数下跌，截至收盘，化工品涨幅居前，苯乙烯涨3.46%；能源品全部上涨，燃油涨2.40%；油脂油料多数上涨，豆一涨1.06%；农副产品跌幅居前，苹果跌4.34%；新能源材料全部下跌，碳酸锂跌3.58%；贵金属全部下跌，钯跌3.48%；基本金属多数下跌，氧化铝跌2.77%；非金属建材涨跌参半，玻璃跌2.59%；黑色系多数下跌，焦炭跌2.49%；航运期货全部下跌，集运指数(欧线)跌1.29%。

多只沪深300ETF尾盘成交额激增

临近尾盘，多只价值风格宽基ETF放量。其中，沪深300ETF华泰柏瑞全天成交146亿元，最后15分钟成交75.94亿元。

沪深300ETF嘉实全天成交106亿元，最后15分钟成交68.47亿元。

上证50ETF华夏全天成交68.08亿元，最后15分钟成交33.77亿元。

从全天来看，沪深300ETF华泰柏瑞、创业板ETF易方达、科创50ETF华夏、沪深300ETF嘉实全天成交额均超过百亿元。

值得注意的是，创业板ETF易方达、科创50ETF华夏、沪深300ETF华泰柏瑞、中证500ETF南方、中证1000ETF南方等的成交额也均超过10月21日全天的成交金额。

据上证报，近期，股票型ETF已连续13个交易日净流入。据Choice测算，9月28日以来，截至10月21日，股票型ETF合计净流入2112.95亿元。宽基ETF成为“吸金”主力，科创50ETF华夏净流入293.98亿元，沪深300ETF华泰柏瑞净流入267.32亿元，创业板ETF易方达净流入265.5亿元，沪深300ETF易方达净流入217.57亿元。

人形机器人/电机/减速器：马斯克"全球最大产业"引爆，多股涨停

大业股份一字涨停、斩获5连板，海洋王同步5连板；兆威机电4天2板；鸣志电器涨停、大洋电机涨停、襄阳轴承涨停、赛福天涨停、安乃达涨停、华新精科涨停、睿能科技涨停、多伦科技涨停。

催化逻辑链密集且重磅，核心是"特斯拉量产时间表正式落地"这一产业级别的叙事升级。

其一，特斯拉Optimus量产时间表落地，马斯克高调定调"全球最大产业"。特斯拉2026年三季度财报披露，公司已在加州弗里蒙特工厂一条大批量产线上开展Optimus人形机器人生产，首批符合量产标准的擎天柱机器人正式下线，现有生产流程已具备商业化产品制造基础；为保障项目落地，特斯拉仅用时46天完成原Model S、Model X生产线拆除改造，该产线面向百万台级生产目标、绝大多数生产设备已部署到位，目前处于早期生产阶段。

马斯克在财报电话会上首次系统摆出量产时间表，并坚信"人形机器人整个赛道都将成为全球最大的产业，未来地球上人形机器人的数量甚至会超过人类"；他预计到明年年末，机器人AI、机电设计、可靠性及使用寿命等问题有望得到解决，"到那个时间点才可以对外向特斯拉以外的企业交付Optimus"；同时计划明年4月左右为Optimus搭载AI5芯片、至少一年后达到周产2万台，2027年底前后可能启动对外交付。特斯拉CFO塔内贾亦表示，未来几年资本开支将继续扩张，用于扩大Optimus产能、采购AI算力基础设施、建设芯片工厂等。

其二，英伟达升级Isaac机器人开发平台。10月21日，英伟达宣布扩展Isaac开放机器人开发平台，新增人形机器人参考平台、数据集、运行时框架及机器人学习工具，推出新的人形机器人参考框架、仿真工作流及数据工具，打通数据生成、模型训练、仿真验证到实际部署全流程，旨在加速通用机器人研发。

其三，宇树世界物理AI大会同日开幕、新品发布。10月22日，2026世界物理AI大会暨宇树合作伙伴生态大会召开，宇树科技创始人王兴兴在主论坛表示，随着GPT-6的发布，物理AI已经看到"被击穿的苗头"，很可能最近1—2年或2—3年具身智能迈过ChatGPT时刻，最核心挑战是AI模型的输入输出与真实机器人的对齐。

他认为基础模型能力的持续跃升将带动物理AI机器人模型自进化循环效能提升，且商业服务的落地会快于家庭、工业领域。宇树科技同步发布新款人形机器人"H2-X（功夫传奇）"，官方视频显示该机器人最长续航约8小时，可徒手抬起汽车、从4米高空平稳落地、一脚踢凹车门。

机构层面普遍看多人形机器人产业，且判断"量产叙事正从口头展望升级为书面+产线+时间表"。情绪接近冰点，2026年10月中旬三季报陆续披露后，A股有望进行主题投资风格切换；机器人流动性、估值、政策、技术、链主等催化大都符合过去七轮机器人上涨行情特征，机器人主题行情当前已具备启动条件；GPT-6与Gemini 4在机器人规划、空间感知及Real-to-Sim建模上的进步正在拓宽通用大模型参与机器人开发的空间，特斯拉有望在四季度发布Optimus V3，看好机器人产业的量产和应用前景。

中泰证券认为本次电话会超预期之处在于给出了相对明确的时间线，短期看交付（核心零部件交付进度、头部供应份额、整机良率、产业链利润贡献），中长期看智能化突破（真机数据飞轮能否持续迭代、应用场景能否持续扩张）。

开源证券指出，物理AI有望成为编码之后需求空间最大的市场，以Optimus为例，落地路径是先工厂、再商用、后家庭，目前Optimus已明确进入量产阶段，2026年10月底上游核心零部件预期达到周产2000—2500台机器人的供应能力，2027年全年保守实现10万台量级，OpenAI、Anthropic、DeepSeek等通用前沿模型公司正酝酿进入具身智能和物理AI。

银行：工建中行齐创历史新高，高股息避险与中期分红共振

在普跌行情中，银行板块午后逆势拉升、局部回暖，成为沪指的重要托底力量。工商银行盘中一度涨超2%、收盘涨1.66%报8.59元，前复权股价刷新历史新高，A+H股总市值约2.86万亿元；建设银行涨1.48%报11.66元、再创历史新高，中国银行亦同步创历史新高；农业银行、渝农商行、兴业银行等跟涨。

items.text:
在美国人工智能（AI）企业专注价格昂贵的闭源模型之际，DeepSeek将自己的技术“家底”向外界开放，赢得海外网友称赞。


10月20日，DeepSeek宣布开源内部生产级推理框架DeepInfer。


该框架是DeepSeek在面临美国尖端芯片出口限制下，确保大模型紧追美国顶尖AI模型的核心。推理框架负责管理模型如何使用计算资源来处理用户请求，其设计会影响延迟、吞吐量以及运行模型所需的硬件，因此是影响AI运营成本的重要因素。

美国彭博社21日指出，推理技术通常被AI公司视为核心竞争力，较少对外公开，而DeepSeek此次公开推理框架，让外界得以一窥其是如何在压低运行成本的同时，确保AI模型性能的。


即使是同一款AI模型，实际运行成本也可能因所采用的软件不同而存在较大差异。更加高效的软件能够降低每次请求所需的计算资源，并有望进一步减少能源消耗。


DeepInfer整合了分布式推理、投机解码等多项技术，能够让AI工作负载分配到不同硬件上，从而让模型在更短时间内生成更多输出，并进一步挖掘芯片的性能。目前，该框架已兼容英伟达SM100 GPU和华为昇腾950 NPU。


这其中不少的底层技术已被业界广泛采用，但DeepSeek针对自身模型进行了专门的优化，使这些技术能够更加高效地协同运行。


美媒称，对于AI托管服务商而言，更低的推理成本意味着更大的利润空间，并有可能进一步转化为更低的AI服务价格。对于企业用户来说，如果选择在自有基础设施上运行DeepSeek模型，DeepInfer也可能帮助其降低算力成本。


不仅如此，DeepSeek开源DeepInfer后，其他开发者也可以研究其中的技术方案，并将部分方法应用到自己的模型推理系统中。


在DeepSeek宣布开源DeepInfer的帖子下方，美国加州一家专注于大语言模型与AI开源优化、本地训练和推理的公司Unsloth AI公开感谢DeepSeek称，其已经借助Dynamic GGUFs，让DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017能够在配备128GB内存的设备上实现本地运行。


评论区还出现了大量海外开发者和AI从业者的积极反馈。一名来自印度的社交媒体博主直接用“Real OPEN AI”（真正的开放AI）评价DeepSeek，并配上一段调侃OpenAI首席执行官山姆·奥尔特曼的视频。

欧洲AI从业者也用漫画嘲讽美国AI公司的闭源模型仅限特定“朋友圈”，与之相对的是中国公司通过降低成本，让AI模型更普惠。

一名来自孟加拉国的软件开发者赞叹说，DeepSeek可能是对开源大语言模型生态贡献最大的公司之一。


当然，DeepSeek此次发布的并不是一套完整的推理技术栈。其文档提到，要构建完整的服务，还需要KV缓存系统、Prefill/Decode解耦，以及在数据并行副本之间进行负载均衡等功能，这些内容并未完全包含在此次开源项目中。不过，大部分核心的解耦功能已经实现。


AI基础设施初创公司Requesty首席执行官蒂博·杰古（Thibault Jaigu）表示，DeepInfer降低了部署DeepSeek模型的门槛，但企业仍需要具备相应的算力和技术能力。他认为，DeepSeek实际上是在告诉外界，“任何人都可以自行托管我们的模型，不过要实现高效的管理，还是有一些技巧需要注意”。


在广大海外网友看来，DeepSeek所做的已不仅仅是发布一个开源推理框架，而是它正在把越来越多原本属于企业内部的技术公开出来，让更多人能够参与进来。这与美国AI行业越来越强调闭源模型、庞大的算力投入和商业护城河的路线形成鲜明对比。


OpenAI的名字里虽然带着“开放”，但其核心模型长期采取闭源策略，反倒是来自中国的DeepSeek正用实际行动践行“开放”一词。


“为善与众行之，为巧与众能之。”正如DeepSeek所说，“我们期待着在不远的未来，能够看到全球AI服务的范围与质量获得前所未有的扩展与提升，变得更加公平、透明、可信赖，进而实现在全社会范围内加快技术迭代、减少能源浪费。”

items.text:
2026年10月19日，Alexandr Wang在社交平台X上发了一张老友合影。


照片里，Meta超级智能实验室的掌舵者Wang、AI编程公司Cognition的创始人Scott Wu，以及加密交易平台Hyperliquid的创始人Jeff Yan，重新聚在了一起。Wang配文只有一句话：“got the HRT gang back together!（HRT帮派重聚！）”

从左到右依次为Jeff Yan、Scott Wu、Alexandr Wang


这是一场跨越十年的重逢。大约十年前，这群从数理竞赛与顶尖名校脱颖而出的年轻人，在量化巨头Hudson River Trading（HRT）的实习办公室里共同研究高频算法；十年后，他们走向了不同的商业高地——Wang创办Scale AI后进入Meta打造明星项目Muse，Wu试图让AI独立编写软件，Yan则在加密金融中打造出明星衍生品平台。当年的实习生，如今已各自成长为影响行业走向的关键造王者。


而在今天的硅谷，这张合影正呈现出另一种意味：同一批人才，正在以惊人的密度进入同一场技术革命，并迅速抵达资本、技术与商业权力的中心。


硅谷曾经有过自己的“PayPal 黑帮”——一批从同一家公司走出的创业者，后来共同塑造了互联网时代。

如今在AI淘金热中，人们开始寻找新的时代群像。只是这一次，站在浪潮前排的面孔，正在发生变化。华人正在潮头涌现。

图片来源社交媒体账号：AYi


顺着这张合影望向整个硅谷，从底层算力芯片、中间数据标注与大模型实验室，再到顶层代码生成与搜索应用，AI各条赛道的核心位置上正密集坐满华人。


在最底层的算力基建，全球四大半导体巨头由华裔统领——英伟达的黄仁勋、AMD的苏姿丰、博通的陈福阳、英特尔的陈立武，牢牢掌控着全球GPU与定制AI芯片的供给命脉。


在中层的数据供应链与前沿实验室，Scale AI的Alexandr Wang与Surge AI的Edwin Chen分割着高质量训练数据的核心市场；Meta超级智能实验室由赵晟佳担任首席科学家，与他对阵的OpenAI则由Mark Chen主导研发大局，xAI的创始技术团队里同样坐着Jimmy Ba和吴宇怀（Yuhuai Wu）等华人核心骨干。


在顶层的商业应用，除了Scott Wu的Cognition，Johnny Ho推动Perplexity估值跃升至数百亿美元并重构搜索体验，Jesse Zhang创办的Decagon拿下数十亿美元客服市场，乔琳创办的Fireworks AI成为开源模型推理的重要中枢，24岁的数学极客Carina Hong则带着Axiom Math冲击机器定理证明。


一栋旧房子里的AI热潮


要理解这种人才密度的来源，不妨先走进一栋住着年轻创业者的普通民宅。


2025年秋天，《Rest of World》记者住进了马克·扎克伯格早年居住过的旧居。这栋位于硅谷洛斯阿尔托斯（Los Altos）的浅蓝色平房，被称为“Facebook House”。二十年前，扎克伯格曾在这里办公，后来打造出社交网络帝国；如今，这里成了新一代华人技术人才的落脚点。


《Rest of World》报道The Chinese whiz kids of Silicon Valley截图


房子里陈设简单，放着床垫、书架与几只猫，却常年举办高密度的AI讨论会。一次聚会中，三十余人围坐交流，院子里烤着整只羊，话题从具身智能、社交产品一直延伸到大模型架构。一位参与聚会的机器人产品经理感叹，周围的气氛已经变成“如果你不做AI，好像就不配活着”。


这种场景揭示了所谓“华人帮”的实际运作机制。


它没有统一的指挥中心，也没有秘密的利益联盟。它首先是一张由共同语言、竞赛履历、海外留学生涯与技术社区织成的人才网络。在这里，刚到湾区的人寻找住处，工程师交换前沿论文的测试细节，创业者寻找技术合伙人。招聘信息和投资线索在重叠的微信群与社交平台X上传播。


当生成式AI成为硅谷最大的资本出口，原本分散在各高校实验室、科技大厂与量化交易机构的人际网络，迅速向商业化阶段汇流。


四位AI创始人，四种不同的命运

Alexandr Wang的命运则走向了“体制化”。他创办的Scale AI曾是全行业通用的数据基础设施。2025年6月，Meta宣布向Scale AI投资约143亿美元，交易对公司的估值超过290亿美元，Wang随后加入Meta统领超级智能实验室。


这笔交易让Wang进入了巨头的权力中枢，却瓦解了Scale AI赖以生存的独立性。 OpenAI与Google出于核心模型资产防泄密的考虑，迅速调整合作，路透社随后披露Google计划削减每年约2亿美元的采购合同。对于一家依靠所有大厂共同哺育的数据服务商来说，失去中立本身就是最大的商业折损。

Edwin Chen选择了另一种赌法。他毕业于麻省理工学院，拥有计算机、数学和语言学学位，曾在Twitter和谷歌负责算法工程。创办Surge AI时，他坚持零外部风投的独立模式：“风投会让公司变得臃肿，还会扭曲团队的激励机制。”根据《The Information》与Sacra披露的数据，Surge AI在2024年依靠约110名全职员工，实现了10亿至12亿美元营收，超过同期拥有千人团队的Scale AI（约8.7亿美元），持续保持盈利，顺理成章承接了大厂外流的数据订单。

在更深层的数理验证领域，24岁的Carina Hong从斯坦福大学博士项目退学，创办定理证明AI公司 Axiom Math，并在2026年3月以超过16亿美元的投后估值完成2亿美元A轮融资。她将知名数学家Ken Ono招募入队，专注利用形式化验证解决大模型在复杂推理中的幻觉问题。她在受访时清晰界定了技术路线：

我们不打算造另一个模仿解答的聊天机器人，我们要教AI去证明定理。这是一个完全不同的挑战。


四个人，四种不同的命运：Wu要把技术轰动变成可靠产品，Wang从创业者走进巨头的权力中心，Chen试图凭借独立性争取市场，Hong则在数学推理的前沿寻找商业出口。


从企业编程、中立数据到定理验证，他们凭借极高的技术判断迅速切入前沿，但在资本与巨头的洗牌下，昔日熟人也不得不面对生硬的市场竞争。


AI实验室阵地与人才争夺


技术产品快速推进的背后，前沿实验室对核心研发人才的争夺同样走向白热化。


2025年年中，扎克伯格亲自出面，连续从OpenAI挖走赵晟佳、余家辉、任泓宇和毕树超四位核心研究员。


这四位技术骨干均在国内名校（清华、中科大少年班、北大、浙大）完成本科教育，随后在斯坦福、UIUC、伯克利获得博士学位。其中，29岁的赵晟佳深度参与了ChatGPT、GPT-4 和 o1逻辑推理模型的架构设计，入职后被任命为Meta超级智能实验室首席科学家。扎克伯格公开表示：

赵晟佳已经开创了包括新扩展范式在内的数项突破，证明了自己是该领域的领军者。

而在OpenAI负责整体技术防守的高级研究副总裁Mark Chen，早年就职于Jane Street，曾与Scott Wu共同担任美国信息学国家队教练。扎克伯格曾私下邀其加盟，遭到Mark Chen拒绝。


为什么是这批人：从奥赛、量化交易到AI实验室


把这些公司和人物串在一起，一个问题自然浮现：为什么这轮AI浪潮里，华裔人才的存在感如此强？


答案不能只归结为“数学好”或“更勤奋”。把这些人物放在一起看，会发现他们的成长路径并不完全相同，却有一些反复出现的交点：数学和计算机训练、顶尖大学、研究机构、量化交易或大型科技公司以及硅谷的创业网络。基础教育阶段严苛的数理奥赛训练打下了底层思维，北美顶尖高校构筑了核心的技术与人脉圈，而在HRT等量化机构与科技大厂的历练，则磨砺出对超高并发架构和极度复杂系统的敏锐直觉。这套路径将极致的数理天赋直接转化为硬核的工程转化力，成为了这一轮AI爆发中最具确定性的孵化器。


比如，Scott Wu的经历与编程和数学竞赛有关；Alexandr Wang以数学能力见长；Carina Hong也从数学兴趣和高强度的技术教育走向AI数学创业。这不是华人独有的路线，但它为理解当前的人才集聚提供了一条线索。


早期华人和印度裔移民也已经在硅谷积累了数十年的技术与创业经验。加州大学伯克利分校学者AnnaLee Saxenian在1999年的研究发现，1998年，华人和印度裔工程师已经在硅谷约四分之一的高科技企业中担任领导角色。今天的AI创业潮并非从零开始，而是建立在长期形成的人才流动和职业网络之上。

中国的教育体系也持续为全球AI研究提供人才。清华姚班、中科大少年班以及重点理工院校数十年来输送的毕业生，在北美形成了厚重的人才蓄水池。


卡内基国际和平基金会（Carnegie China）2026年9月发布的全球 AI 人才追踪研报《Who’s Ahead in the Global AI Talent Race?》显示：在全球顶尖AI研究人员中，多达57%在中国的高校完成了本科阶段教育，这一比例相比2022年的46%跃升了11个百分点；同期美国本土本科培养的人才占比则下滑至 13%。该研究写道：

中国已确立作为全球精英人工智能人才最大来源国的显著领先地位。


Carnegie 研究，以NeurIPS论文作者10280人为样本


这个口径衡量的是教育背景，不是华人族裔或国籍，也不能直接代表整个AI行业；但它提示，中国培养的人才与美国等地的研究和就业机会之间，存在重要联系。


产业界同样感受到了这种人才厚度。英伟达CEO黄仁勋在接受《Axios》访谈时就直言“全球一半的AI研究人员是华人”。

美国科技产业的吸引力，则让一部分人才有机会把研究能力转化成创业机会。投资人、早期员工和潜在客户可以通过共同的学校、前雇主和行业聚会相互连接。“Facebook House”这样的空间，正是这张网络在日常生活中的一个缩影。


不过，这并不意味着华裔在商业上占据全面主导。但放眼这一轮生成式AI浪潮，其他族裔的身影确实远不如华人密集。欧美精英大多停留在上一波的资本与愿景叙事中，印度裔则更多走的是大企业CEO路线——纳德拉、皮查伊皆是如此——而非创业领军人物或首席科学家的路线。东欧与俄裔科学家在理论探索上仍有突破，但批量涌现创业者与核心研发骨干的，是华人。


为什么是现在？AI让创业者更早走到舞台中央


回到Scott Wu与Carina Hong的案例，这一轮技术周期深刻改变了技术人才进入商业的路径。


十年前，开发复杂软件需要雇佣庞大的人力搭建工具链与基础设施，经历漫长开发才能推向市场。现在的底层大模型通过API输出了通用的推理能力，云厂商提供了现成的算力底座，初创团队可以将精力完全集中在调度优化、提示工程与专业交付上。


一个小团队不必自建底层模型，就能开发编程Agent或定理验证系统。这大幅拉低了技术原型的启动门槛，使得拥有极强数学与代码优化能力的工程小团队，能在数月内推出支撑企业采购的产品。


但这种速度也是一把双刃剑：应用层容易启动，巨头的跟进同样迅速。产品一旦被上游模型平台吸收，独立创企就必须承受巨大的生存挤压。技术突破只是拿到了入场券，如何不被平台吞噬才是长久命题。


两代华人，两种路径


如果只看年轻创业者，容易误以为华裔在硅谷的崛起始于生成式AI。实际上，黄仁勋、苏姿丰等老一代华裔掌门人早已在芯片产业筑起硬件壁垒。黄仁勋掌管英伟达，苏姿丰执掌 AMD，陈福阳（Hock Tan）掌舵博通，创投老兵陈立武出任英特尔CEO。


黄仁勋、苏姿丰、陈立武公开活动照片拼接


但两代人的路径截然不同：老一代靠数十年的制造、供应链与生态积累产业权力，新一代则在现成算力之上，以极高的资本效率快速切入应用层。年轻一代融到的巨额资金，绝大多数最终流向英伟达、AMD与博通的数据中心——软件速度始终依附于硬件基础。


硅谷的历史里，移民一直是重要的推动力量。不同年代，来自不同地区的人才通过教育、研究、工程和创业进入核心位置。


今天的AI浪潮，让一批华人背景的研究者和创业者再次走到了聚光灯下。只是这一次，前排的面孔变了。


而这一轮AI淘金热中，批量涌向潮头的，是华人。他们不是同一个“帮派”，却共享着相似的训练、网络与野心。真正值得追问的，不是他们如何竞争，而是这张华人人才网络，将如何定义下一阶段的硅谷。

Edwin Chen选择了另一种赌法。他毕业于麻省理工学院，拥有计算机、数学和语言学学位，曾在Twitter和谷歌负责算法工程。创办Surge AI时，他坚持零外部风投的独立模式：“风投会让公司变得臃肿，还会扭曲团队的激励机制。”根据《The Information》与Sacra披露的数据，Surge AI在2024年依靠约110名全职员工，实现了10亿至12亿美元营收，超过同期拥有千人团队的Scale AI（约8.7亿美元），持续保持盈利，顺理成章承接了大厂外流的数据订单。
在更深层的数理验证领域，24岁的Carina Hong从斯坦福大学博士项目退学，创办定理证明AI公司 Axiom Math，并在2026年3月以超过16亿美元的投后估值完成2亿美元A轮融资。她将知名数学家Ken Ono招募入队，专注利用形式化验证解决大模型在复杂推理中的幻觉问题。她在受访时清晰界定了技术路线：
我们不打算造另一个模仿解答的聊天机器人，我们要教AI去证明定理。这是一个完全不同的挑战。
四个人，四种不同的命运：Wu要把技术轰动变成可靠产品，Wang从创业者走进巨头的权力中心，Chen试图凭借独立性争取市场，Hong则在数学推理的前沿寻找商业出口。
从企业编程、中立数据到定理验证，他们凭借极高的技术判断迅速切入前沿，但在资本与巨头的洗牌下，昔日熟人也不得不面对生硬的市场竞争。
AI实验室阵地与人才争夺
技术产品快速推进的背后，前沿实验室对核心研发人才的争夺同样走向白热化。
2025年年中，扎克伯格亲自出面，连续从OpenAI挖走赵晟佳、余家辉、任泓宇和毕树超四位核心研究员。
这四位技术骨干均在国内名校（清华、中科大少年班、北大、浙大）完成本科教育，随后在斯坦福、UIUC、伯克利获得博士学位。其中，29岁的赵晟佳深度参与了ChatGPT、GPT-4 和 o1逻辑推理模型的架构设计，入职后被任命为Meta超级智能实验室首席科学家。扎克伯格公开表示：
赵晟佳已经开创了包括新扩展范式在内的数项突破，证明了自己是该领域的领军者。
而在OpenAI负责整体技术防守的高级研究副总裁Mark Chen，早年就职于Jane Street，曾与Scott Wu共同担任美国信息学国家队教练。扎克伯格曾私下邀其加盟，遭到Mark Chen拒绝。
为什么是这批人：从奥赛、量化交易到AI实验室
把这些公司和人物串在一起，一个问题自然浮现：为什么这轮AI浪潮里，华裔人才的存在感如此强？

答案不能只归结为“数学好”或“更勤奋”。把这些人物放在一起看，会发现他们的成长路径并不完全相同，却有一些反复出现的交点：数学和计算机训练、顶尖大学、研究机构、量化交易或大型科技公司以及硅谷的创业网络。基础教育阶段严苛的数理奥赛训练打下了底层思维，北美顶尖高校构筑了核心的技术与人脉圈，而在HRT等量化机构与科技大厂的历练，则磨砺出对超高并发架构和极度复杂系统的敏锐直觉。这套路径将极致的数理天赋直接转化为硬核的工程转化力，成为了这一轮AI爆发中最具确定性的孵化器。
比如，Scott Wu的经历与编程和数学竞赛有关；Alexandr Wang以数学能力见长；Carina Hong也从数学兴趣和高强度的技术教育走向AI数学创业。这不是华人独有的路线，但它为理解当前的人才集聚提供了一条线索。
早期华人和印度裔移民也已经在硅谷积累了数十年的技术与创业经验。加州大学伯克利分校学者AnnaLee Saxenian在1999年的研究发现，1998年，华人和印度裔工程师已经在硅谷约四分之一的高科技企业中担任领导角色。今天的AI创业潮并非从零开始，而是建立在长期形成的人才流动和职业网络之上。
中国的教育体系也持续为全球AI研究提供人才。清华姚班、中科大少年班以及重点理工院校数十年来输送的毕业生，在北美形成了厚重的人才蓄水池。
卡内基国际和平基金会（Carnegie China）2026年9月发布的全球 AI 人才追踪研报《Who’s Ahead in the Global AI Talent Race?》显示：在全球顶尖AI研究人员中，多达57%在中国的高校完成了本科阶段教育，这一比例相比2022年的46%跃升了11个百分点；同期美国本土本科培养的人才占比则下滑至 13%。该研究写道：
中国已确立作为全球精英人工智能人才最大来源国的显著领先地位。
Carnegie 研究，以NeurIPS论文作者10280人为样本
这个口径衡量的是教育背景，不是华人族裔或国籍，也不能直接代表整个AI行业；但它提示，中国培养的人才与美国等地的研究和就业机会之间，存在重要联系。
产业界同样感受到了这种人才厚度。英伟达CEO黄仁勋在接受《Axios》访谈时就直言“全球一半的AI研究人员是华人”。
美国科技产业的吸引力，则让一部分人才有机会把研究能力转化成创业机会。投资人、早期员工和潜在客户可以通过共同的学校、前雇主和行业聚会相互连接。“Facebook House”这样的空间，正是这张网络在日常生活中的一个缩影。
不过，这并不意味着华裔在商业上占据全面主导。但放眼这一轮生成式AI浪潮，其他族裔的身影确实远不如华人密集。欧美精英大多停留在上一波的资本与愿景叙事中，印度裔则更多走的是大企业CEO路线——纳德拉、皮查伊皆是如此——而非创业领军人物或首席科学家的路线。东欧与俄裔科学家在理论探索上仍有突破，但批量涌现创业者与核心研发骨干的，是华人。
为什么是现在？AI让创业者更早走到舞台中央
回到Scott Wu与Carina Hong的案例，这一轮技术周期深刻改变了技术人才进入商业的路径。
十年前，开发复杂软件需要雇佣庞大的人力搭建工具链与基础设施，经历漫长开发才能推向市场。现在的底层大模型通过API输出了通用的推理能力，云厂商提供了现成的算力底座，初创团队可以将精力完全集中在调度优化、提示工程与专业交付上。
一个小团队不必自建底层模型，就能开发编程Agent或定理验证系统。这大幅拉低了技术原型的启动门槛，使得拥有极强数学与代码优化能力的工程小团队，能在数月内推出支撑企业采购的产品。
但这种速度也是一把双刃剑：应用层容易启动，巨头的跟进同样迅速。产品一旦被上游模型平台吸收，独立创企就必须承受巨大的生存挤压。技术突破只是拿到了入场券，如何不被平台吞噬才是长久命题。
两代华人，两种路径
如果只看年轻创业者，容易误以为华裔在硅谷的崛起始于生成式AI。实际上，黄仁勋、苏姿丰等老一代华裔掌门人早已在芯片产业筑起硬件壁垒。黄仁勋掌管英伟达，苏姿丰执掌 AMD，陈福阳（Hock Tan）掌舵博通，创投老兵陈立武出任英特尔CEO。
黄仁勋、苏姿丰、陈立武公开活动照片拼接
但两代人的路径截然不同：老一代靠数十年的制造、供应链与生态积累产业权力，新一代则在现成算力之上，以极高的资本效率快速切入应用层。年轻一代融到的巨额资金，绝大多数最终流向英伟达、AMD与博通的数据中心——软件速度始终依附于硬件基础。
硅谷的历史里，移民一直是重要的推动力量。不同年代，来自不同地区的人才通过教育、研究、工程和创业进入核心位置。
今天的AI浪潮，让一批华人背景的研究者和创业者再次走到了聚光灯下。只是这一次，前排的面孔变了。
而这一轮AI淘金热中，批量涌向潮头的，是华人。他们不是同一个“帮派”，却共享着相似的训练、网络与野心。真正值得追问的，不是他们如何竞争，而是这张华人人才网络，将如何定义下一阶段的硅谷。

items.title: 野村警告：当前AI信用风险与互联网泡沫、雷曼危机前惊人相似，一切都取决于油价

items.text:
野村证券发出警告，当前围绕美国科技公司和法国的信用动荡，与2000年互联网泡沫崩溃和2008年雷曼危机前夕的信用冲击高度相似，历史上每一次“第二轮冲击”之后约一至两年，都演变为引发衰退的“第三轮冲击”。这一次，油价走势将成为决定历史是否重演的关键变量。


野村证券策略师Naka Matsuzawa在10月22日发布的报告中指出，当前信用市场的不安情绪，令人联想到1990年代IT繁荣期间的亚洲货币危机与LTCM危机，以及2000年代房地产繁荣期间的次贷危机与贝尔斯登危机。这些事件均属于其所定义的十年信用周期中的“第二轮冲击”。历史表明，若美联储能够及时转向降息，经济可在不经历全面信用危机的情况下重返扩张轨道；但若油价因经济过热而非地缘政治因素上涨，央行政策空间将被大幅压缩，信用危机将难以避免。


Matsuzawa警告称，美欧央行目前正因油价上涨而持续加息，这一背景与历史上“第三轮冲击”前夕的滞胀困境如出一辙，意味着当前的信用隐忧存在从局部风险演变为系统性危机的可能。不过，若油价上涨的驱动力主要来自地缘政治而非需求端，美联储仍有政策灵活性，可在冲击发生后暂停加息，从而阻断危机升级。


历史镜鉴：两次“第二轮冲击”如何演变为系统性危机


Matsuzawa在报告中构建了一套十年信用周期框架，将历史上的重大信用事件划分为“第二轮冲击”与“第三轮冲击”两个阶段。


第二轮冲击通常规模有限，尚不足以引发全面衰退。1997年亚洲货币危机和1998年LTCM危机，均发生在1990年代IT繁荣周期之中；2007年次贷危机和贝尔斯登危机，则发生在2000年代房地产繁荣周期之中。这两组事件均属于第二轮冲击，均未直接导致全面信用危机或经济衰退。

关键的转折点在于央行的政策应对。报告指出，在上述两次第二轮冲击发生时，通胀压力和“政策落后于曲线”的担忧尚不突出，美联储因此得以迅速暂停加息并转向降息，成功将信用收缩扼杀于萌芽状态，经济随之重返扩张轨道。


然而，在随后约一至两年的扩张之后，更大规模的“第三轮冲击”相继爆发——2000年互联网泡沫崩溃和2008年雷曼危机——并最终引发经济衰退。报告特别指出，在这两次第三轮冲击发生时，美联储均无法在冲击发生后立即实施货币宽松，政策被迫滞后，加剧了危机的烈度。


油价：决定央行政策空间的核心变量


Matsuzawa将原油价格定性为衡量美联储政策灵活性的核心指标，也是判断当前信用隐忧能否被遏制的关键所在。


逻辑链条清晰：当油价因经济过热或通胀压力上涨时，央行面临滞胀困境——既要应对信用冲击，又无法降息刺激经济，政策空间被双重挤压。这正是历史上第三轮冲击得以演变为系统性危机的根本原因。


报告明确指出，美欧央行目前正因油价上涨而持续加息，市场已将美国和欧洲12月加息的概率定价为接近100%，日本12月加息概率亦接近80%。这一政策取向与历史上第三轮冲击前夕的宏观背景高度吻合，构成当前最值得警惕的风险信号。


然而，报告也提供了一个相对乐观的情景：若油价上涨的主要驱动力来自地缘政治因素而非需求端，则美联储仍可在信用冲击发生后保留降息空间，从而重演1997年至1998年和2007年的历史——以政策转向阻断危机升级，将第二轮冲击控制在可管理范围之内。


当前市场信号：信用隐忧持续，风险偏好分化


报告发布当日，市场呈现出信用隐忧与风险偏好并存的复杂格局，印证了野村对当前处于“第二轮冲击”阶段的判断。


在信用市场，美国科技公司CDS利差有所收窄，但法德国债利差持续走阔，显示欧洲主权信用压力尚未缓解。美债和德债收益率曲线均呈现扭曲式平坦化——短端和中端债券因加息预期升温而走弱，长端债券则持续受到避险资金追捧。


在股票市场，美国科技股和资本品股因企业财报表现强劲而领涨，银行股虽有反弹但明显落后，防御性板块和消费相关板块表现平淡。科技股与银行股的分化，折射出市场对AI驱动的增长叙事与信用风险之间张力的真实定价。


在大宗商品市场，油价和铜价双双下跌，比特币和黄金则走高。市场波动率指标方面，MOVE指数降至95.9，VIX降至16.7，美元兑日元波动率指数亦降至7.1，整体波动率处于相对温和水平。日元在158.0至158.5区间内窄幅震荡，缺乏独立驱动因素。


对日本市场的传导：债券受益，股市跟随


Matsuzawa在报告中对日本市场的短期走势作出研判，认为日本资产将主要跟随海外市场节奏，但信用隐忧的持续发酵值得关注。


日本国债有望受益于美欧长端国债上涨和油价回落。法德国债利差所反映的持续信用担忧，预计将继续推动资金流向长期国债避险。与此同时，尽管油价昨日下跌，美欧加息预期仍小幅回升，日本市场是否跟随这一趋势值得密切观察。


日本股市则有望受到美欧股市走强和油价下跌的双重支撑。报告指出，市场关注焦点将集中于银行股能否与科技股同步反弹——在美欧市场，两者昨日均有上涨，但信用隐忧仍如法德国债利差所示持续存在，银行股的修复力度因此受到制约。


值得注意的是，日本12月加息概率已被市场定价至接近80%，这意味着日本货币政策正逐步向美欧靠拢，一旦全球信用风险进一步升级，日本央行的政策灵活性同样将面临考验。

Matsuzawa警告称，美欧央行目前正因油价上涨而持续加息，这一背景与历史上“第三轮冲击”前夕的滞胀困境如出一辙，意味着当前的信用隐忧存在从局部风险演变为系统性危机的可能。不过，若油价上涨的驱动力主要来自地缘政治而非需求端，美联储仍有政策灵活性，可在冲击发生后暂停加息，从而阻断危机升级。
历史镜鉴：两次“第二轮冲击”如何演变为系统性危机
Matsuzawa在报告中构建了一套十年信用周期框架，将历史上的重大信用事件划分为“第二轮冲击”与“第三轮冲击”两个阶段。
第二轮冲击通常规模有限，尚不足以引发全面衰退。1997年亚洲货币危机和1998年LTCM危机，均发生在1990年代IT繁荣周期之中；2007年次贷危机和贝尔斯登危机，则发生在2000年代房地产繁荣周期之中。这两组事件均属于第二轮冲击，均未直接导致全面信用危机或经济衰退。
关键的转折点在于央行的政策应对。报告指出，在上述两次第二轮冲击发生时，通胀压力和“政策落后于曲线”的担忧尚不突出，美联储因此得以迅速暂停加息并转向降息，成功将信用收缩扼杀于萌芽状态，经济随之重返扩张轨道。
然而，在随后约一至两年的扩张之后，更大规模的“第三轮冲击”相继爆发——2000年互联网泡沫崩溃和2008年雷曼危机——并最终引发经济衰退。报告特别指出，在这两次第三轮冲击发生时，美联储均无法在冲击发生后立即实施货币宽松，政策被迫滞后，加剧了危机的烈度。
油价：决定央行政策空间的核心变量
Matsuzawa将原油价格定性为衡量美联储政策灵活性的核心指标，也是判断当前信用隐忧能否被遏制的关键所在。
逻辑链条清晰：当油价因经济过热或通胀压力上涨时，央行面临滞胀困境——既要应对信用冲击，又无法降息刺激经济，政策空间被双重挤压。这正是历史上第三轮冲击得以演变为系统性危机的根本原因。
报告明确指出，美欧央行目前正因油价上涨而持续加息，市场已将美国和欧洲12月加息的概率定价为接近100%，日本12月加息概率亦接近80%。这一政策取向与历史上第三轮冲击前夕的宏观背景高度吻合，构成当前最值得警惕的风险信号。
然而，报告也提供了一个相对乐观的情景：若油价上涨的主要驱动力来自地缘政治因素而非需求端，则美联储仍可在信用冲击发生后保留降息空间，从而重演1997年至1998年和2007年的历史——以政策转向阻断危机升级，将第二轮冲击控制在可管理范围之内。
当前市场信号：信用隐忧持续，风险偏好分化
报告发布当日，市场呈现出信用隐忧与风险偏好并存的复杂格局，印证了野村对当前处于“第二轮冲击”阶段的判断。
在信用市场，美国科技公司CDS利差有所收窄，但法德国债利差持续走阔，显示欧洲主权信用压力尚未缓解。美债和德债收益率曲线均呈现扭曲式平坦化——短端和中端债券因加息预期升温而走弱，长端债券则持续受到避险资金追捧。
在股票市场，美国科技股和资本品股因企业财报表现强劲而领涨，银行股虽有反弹但明显落后，防御性板块和消费相关板块表现平淡。科技股与银行股的分化，折射出市场对AI驱动的增长叙事与信用风险之间张力的真实定价。
在大宗商品市场，油价和铜价双双下跌，比特币和黄金则走高。市场波动率指标方面，MOVE指数降至95.9，VIX降至16.7，美元兑日元波动率指数亦降至7.1，整体波动率处于相对温和水平。日元在158.0至158.5区间内窄幅震荡，缺乏独立驱动因素。
对日本市场的传导：债券受益，股市跟随
Matsuzawa在报告中对日本市场的短期走势作出研判，认为日本资产将主要跟随海外市场节奏，但信用隐忧的持续发酵值得关注。
日本国债有望受益于美欧长端国债上涨和油价回落。法德国债利差所反映的持续信用担忧，预计将继续推动资金流向长期国债避险。与此同时，尽管油价昨日下跌，美欧加息预期仍小幅回升，日本市场是否跟随这一趋势值得密切观察。
日本股市则有望受到美欧股市走强和油价下跌的双重支撑。报告指出，市场关注焦点将集中于银行股能否与科技股同步反弹——在美欧市场，两者昨日均有上涨，但信用隐忧仍如法德国债利差所示持续存在，银行股的修复力度因此受到制约。
值得注意的是，日本12月加息概率已被市场定价至接近80%，这意味着日本货币政策正逐步向美欧靠拢，一旦全球信用风险进一步升级，日本央行的政策灵活性同样将面临考验。

items.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
items.summary: At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's
items.text:
At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.

I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.

These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.

"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Meanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition.

It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.

A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime.

In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for.

Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.

In Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November.

No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction.

"It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.

The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness."

"As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."

This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.

The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.

With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.

The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

items.text:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".

Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.

Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.

Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.

They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.

The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.

Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.

He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.

Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.

"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.

items.text:
Earlier today, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. These releases fix two critical vulnerabilities that, under the right conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems.

This post isn't about how to update. It's about how these vulnerabilities were found and fixed, what has changed in how PHP security is handled over the past two years, and what we need from the organizations that depend on PHP to keep PHP's security work going.

CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w: RCE via OOM corruption (out-of-memory): If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory. On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings. Remote code execution was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths.

CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp: RCE via stale global state: A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request. A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.

Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.

A first external audit and increased security focus

In 2024, PHP underwent its first external security audit in years. The PHP Foundation secured funding from the Sovereign Tech Agency to organize this audit through OSTIF, and it was carried out by Quarkslab. While fixing one of the issues Quarkslab reported, a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618. In 2024, a potential exploit for the OOM problem was theorized, but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.

To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs: backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources. The security team has since started changing its processes, and that work continues, so that decisions can be made by majority and compromises are encouraged.

Building a sustainable professional security organization

Over the last months the way PHP security work is organized has changed considerably. In May 2026, the PHP Foundation created the Ecosystem Security Team, which works alongside the PHP security team on triage, coordination, and hardening. Volker Dusch's work as AI Security Engineer in Residence at the PHP Foundation has significantly improved communication and collaboration between the PHP security team and the Foundation. Alexandre Daubois joined the PHP Foundation in July to help the PHP security team triage, handle, and fix security reports and Daniel Scherzer joined in September to take on hardening work.

Earlier this year, we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos. But since the Mythos scan, we have added other tools, including OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits, alongside sanitizer builds and reproduction environments that match our CI on every platform PHP supports.

The PHP Foundation got the PHP project into the Patch the Planet program, as part of which security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026. On August 11th researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on the same day, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th. More recently, Trail of Bits has also been auditing PHP. The reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz made the full impact of the OOM problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation's team working on security. Without the Foundation’s funding it would have been impossible to have multiple people work on this issue full time, eventually through weekends and around the clock to coordinate and communicate with other involved parties.

The growth of AI-assisted research also means the PHP security team receives far more reports than before. As Alexandre Daubois described last week in How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports, the team has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible. AI helps the team validate reports and group reports sharing the same root cause, but a person makes every call and works on every patch.

Leak and disrupted disclosure

The coordinated disclosure of these vulnerabilities worked well until 2 days ahead of the targeted release date.

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC. Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update. Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.

As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues, mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well. The PHP security team closely monitored and inspected appearing PoCs after the leak but did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.

On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.

A cautiously optimistic outlook

Today's release shows the progress we’re making in how PHP security is handled. Once the full impact of the OOM problem was understood in August, the security team, the foundation, and the release managers delivered a fix for this deeply rooted problem across all supported branches, and distributions and LTS vendors received the patch ahead of time so their users can update quickly.

We are confident that a serious vulnerability with a fix stuck on hard trade-offs would now reach the PHP Foundation leadership much sooner, as we’re changing processes so leadership can help steer the situation to a timely resolution. We are now prioritizing measures to make sure vulnerabilities that need similarly complex fixes get resolved faster when they are reported in the future. The PHP Foundation and the PHP security team learned a lot in the last weeks and will work to turn their experiences into lasting repeatable processes.

What we need from you

PHP runs a large share of the web, including government services, online stores, banks, media sites, and much of the software that businesses rely on every day. Yet security work on PHP itself still depends on a small group of foundation-funded developers and a little volunteer help.

Tools now find bugs faster than ever, for defenders and attackers alike, and the number of reports will keep growing. What tools cannot do is decide on the right fix for a long-standing design decision in the engine, weigh the compatibility trade-offs, and review the patch. Making those decisions takes experienced engineers who know the entire PHP codebase, and today there are too few of them.

A core part of the PHP Foundation's mission is to grow the number of engineers with deep knowledge of the PHP codebase and give the security team the resources it needs. We can only achieve this goal with funding from those who depend on PHP:

Companies that build products and services on PHP: please sponsor the PHP Foundation at a level that reflects how much you rely on it.

Hosting providers, cloud platforms, and distributions that deliver PHP to millions of users.

Governments and public institutions whose services run on PHP. The German Sovereign Tech Agency's funding of the 2024 audit shows what public investment can achieve, and we need more of it, on a sustained basis.

Sponsoring the PHP Foundation is the most direct way to ensure structural issues like the OOM vulnerability are addressed sustainably, before they turn into emergencies. Become a sponsor at thephp.foundation/sponsor, and if your organization would like to talk about a larger commitment, get in touch.

Thank you

Thank you to the PHP security team, volunteers and PHP Foundation contractors alike, the release managers, and the package maintainers at distributions and LTS vendors who made these releases possible. Thank you to Calif, especially Ryan A, Wiz, OpenAI Codex Security, especially Amy Burnett, OSTIF, and Quarkslab for their research and responsible disclosure; to Alpha-Omega, OpenAI, and Anthropic for giving the team access to their tools and funding some of the security work; to the Sovereign Tech Agency for funding the 2024 audit; and to all of our sponsors, whose support made this work possible.
